segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: TUTOR Well, good afternoon.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: In today's session John Upton will be sharing some of the findings of his research project from last term.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: John ...

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: Thanks.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: Well, first of all, a little bit about the background to the project.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: Our title, as you can see, is pretty straightforward: 'car safety'.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: But these days there's a lot more to it than the usual injunctions about drinking and driving or speeding.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: I had been interested and horrified by several newspaper reports on what people call 'road rage'.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: For the famous incident of a man getting out of his car in a car park and hitting the driver of a van who had overtaken him earlier.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: It seemed to me that there were almost as many serious problems when cars were parked ... i.e. were stationary ... as when they were travelling at 90 miles an hour.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: So I decided to make this the focus of the project.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: For our research we depended mainly on talking to individuals, asking them questions rather than using written questionnaires.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: We stopped people at a selected garage on the motorway over a two-day period, and asked them questions about what they'd observed or experienced themselves.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: Our respondents were both men and women, but the women were just slightly in the majority.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: We were pleased by the public's willingness to stop and chat to us ... in the end we talked to a total of 135 drivers over those two days.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: So what were our findings?

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: Well, as you can see, 93% of respondents had had some kind of problem.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: A surprisingly large percentage - 24% had had their car damaged in some way, but the main type of incident was being shouted at - 79% had experienced that. 15% had experienced violence on their own persons ... they'd actually been hit by someone.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: The police tended only to be informed when there was physical violence involved.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: So what strategies had people developed to ensure their own safety?

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: Let's have a look at the figures here.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: Well, first of all, it was quite striking that there were often distinct answers from the men and women.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: It was mainly women, for , who said one shouldn't ever stop to find out how to get somewhere.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: Whereas it was men who said you should try to avoid looking directly at other drivers.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: Both men and ... oh sorry n o . . . it was women who said you had to tell someone when you were due to get to a particular destination.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: Then, I had thought that it would be mainly men, but both sexes made the point that it's much safer to get keys out well in advance as you go towards your car.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: Men were very aware that muggers or whatever might be concealed behind the car.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: They also made the point that you should leave plenty of room when you park your car so you can make a quick getaway if you need to.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: Finally, locking doors at all times ... men didn't think it was quite as important as women, but both gave it a high safety rating.

segments.speaker: JOHN
segments.en: When we asked them what they thought the best improvements had been in the last five years in helping with road rage problems ...
